text: Amazon CloudWatch is AWS's answer to everything Azure Monitor does for Azure — the platform that collects metrics from every AWS service, and the place you build alarms on top of them. If Northbridge Retail runs checkout on AWS instead, CloudWatch is where that story starts.

The overview page surfaces alarm states and metric graphs together, so you can triage without digging into one specific service first. Every metric lives inside a namespace tied to the service that published it, like AWS/EC2 or AWS/ApplicationELB, and dimensions let you scope that metric down to one specific resource, like one load balancer, instead of an undifferentiated average across everything you own.

A static threshold alarm compares a metric against a fixed number you choose — fine when you know the acceptable range in advance. But request volume during a flash sale has a normal range that shifts by time of day and day of week, so anomaly detection has CloudWatch learn the expected pattern over about two weeks and draw a dynamic band around it instead, firing only when the metric actually leaves that band, not when it crosses one fixed line.

Every CloudWatch alarm sits in exactly one of three states: OK, meaning the metric's within its defined range; ALARM, meaning it's breached the threshold; or INSUFFICIENT_DATA, meaning there isn't enough data yet to know — which is common right after you create an alarm, and not itself a sign that anything's broken.

Namespaces, dimensions, static or anomaly-based thresholds, and three clean alarm states — that's the core of CloudWatch monitoring. Next up, lesson eleven: CloudWatch Logs and Insights, for querying the detail behind exactly what an alarm is telling you.
